selection_weights_approval.basis: reuses the Study 1 version-selection weighting for consistency

questions.question_text: Before you started trying to conceive, what did you expect the process of getting support or guidance from healthcare professionals to look like? And thinking back now, what did that support actually look like in reality?

probes.probe_text: What was the biggest surprise — positive or negative — when you first engaged with a healthcare provider about trying to conceive?
Was there anything you felt you needed in that early stage that no one offered or even asked about?
How did it feel when your expectations met — or didn't meet — what actually happened?

probes.text: When you think about the advice or reassurances you were given during that time — were there moments where something just felt right, or where something quietly didn't sit well with you, even if you couldn't explain why?
Was there ever a moment where you found yourself double-checking something a provider told you — maybe looking it up later, or asking someone else — and if so, what prompted that?

questions.question_text: If you had a pre-existing health condition before pregnancy, what did you expect the healthcare system to do to help you prepare? And what actually happened when you sought that help?

probes.probe_text: Did you feel you had to advocate strongly for yourself, or did the system proactively reach out to support you?
What was missing from the care you received at this stage that would have made a real difference?
How did it feel to navigate your health condition alongside the desire to conceive?

probes.text: When you were managing your health condition alongside trying to conceive, was there anyone in the system who felt like they were holding the full picture of what you were going through — or did it feel more like different pieces of you were with different people?

questions.question_text: If you experienced a previous pregnancy loss, what did you expect the healthcare system to offer you when you decided to try again? And what support was actually available to you?

probes.probe_text: Was there a point where you felt your previous loss was not being taken seriously enough in the context of your new pregnancy attempt?
What was the biggest thing missing from the care or information you received at this stage?
Where did you turn for support that the formal healthcare system wasn't providing?

probes.text: After your loss, when you were ready to try again — did you feel like the people supporting you had any memory of what you'd already been through, or did it feel like you were starting from the beginning again?

questions.question_text: When you first found out you were pregnant, what did you expect your first antenatal appointments to be like — the environment, the people, the information you'd receive? And what were they actually like?

probes.probe_text: What was the biggest surprise — positive or negative — about those first appointments?
Did you feel listened to in those early appointments, or did you feel processed? What created that feeling?
Was there anything about the physical environment or the way the service was set up that made it harder or easier for you to engage?

probes.text: Can you take me back to a moment during your care — it could be something small, like the way a midwife or doctor walked into the room, or how they spoke to your partner or support person — where you left feeling either really seen as a person, or somehow… less than that? What was happening around you when that feeling came up?

questions.question_text: Before your screening tests and scans, what did you expect the process of understanding your results to be like — how information would be given, by whom, and in what way? And what was the reality?

probes.probe_text: Was there a gap between the amount of information you were given and the amount you felt you needed to make sense of your results?
Did you turn to other sources — apps, online forums, friends — to understand what you'd been told? What drove that?
Were there moments during this process where you felt your values or wishes weren't being taken into account?

probes.text: When you got your results and you were waiting to speak to someone — what did that in-between time feel like, and did you find anything that helped you sit with it?
Did you ever feel like you'd already half-answered your own question before the midwife or doctor had a chance to explain it? What had taken you there?
Looking back, was there a version of the information you needed that felt like it was written for someone like you — or did you have to piece something together yourself from different places?

questions.question_text: During your pregnancy, what did you expect in terms of having a consistent midwife or care provider who knew your history and situation? And what continuity of care did you actually experience?

probes.probe_text: What was the impact — practically or emotionally — of seeing different providers at different appointments?
Were there times you had to repeat your history or concerns because they weren't carried forward? How did that feel?
Did the fragmentation of care — if you experienced it — affect how much you trusted the system overall?

probes.text: Looking back, was there ever a moment when you felt like someone in your care team really *knew* you — your whole story, not just what was written on a form that day? What was that like compared to the other appointments?

If you imagine the person who saw you very early on in your pregnancy, and then the people who were there at the end — how much of *you* do you think travelled with you through that journey, from their perspective?
Were there things you found yourself explaining again and again — to different people, at different appointments — that you'd hoped wouldn't need repeating? How did that land for you at the time?
Over the course of your appointments, did you ever find yourself holding back something you wanted to say or ask — and if you did, what made you hesitate in that moment?

Thinking about the different people who cared for you through your pregnancy — did you ever feel like some of them really had a picture of your whole situation, and others perhaps only had a piece of it? What was that like to navigate?

questions.question_text: Before labour, what did you expect your pain management options to be — the range available, how they'd be offered, and how you'd be supported in deciding? And what was the reality of pain management during your labour?

probes.probe_text: Were there pain management options you wanted but weren't able to access? What got in the way?
How did it feel when the pain experience differed from what you had expected or prepared for?
Did you feel your pain was taken seriously and responded to promptly? What shaped that impression?

probes.text: During labour, there can be a lot happening very fast. Were there times when you felt like decisions about your body were moving ahead of you — before you'd had a chance to catch up with what was being suggested? What was that like?

Before your labour, you may have had a sense of how you wanted to feel in your body during that time — in control, informed, prepared in a certain way. How close did the reality get to that picture, and where did it differ?

questions.question_text: If your birth involved an unexpected intervention or complication, what did you expect the process of being informed and involved in those decisions to look like? And how were those decisions actually made and communicated in the moment?

probes.probe_text: Did you feel you had genuine choice and sufficient information in those moments, or did decisions feel like they happened to you rather than with you?
What was missing — in terms of explanation, tone, or timing — that would have helped you feel more respected in those moments?
Looking back, did those decisions and the way they were handled affect your ability to trust healthcare providers afterward?

questions.question_text: Before birth, what did you expect the immediate period after your baby was born to be like — skin-to-skin contact, who would be present, what would be done? And what actually happened in those first moments after delivery?

probes.probe_text: Was there anything that happened — or didn't happen — in those first moments that still stays with you? What was it?
Did clinical priorities override your personal wishes in those moments? How was that handled?
Was your partner or support person included in the way you had hoped in those immediate post-birth moments?

questions.question_text: Before your baby arrived, what did you expect feeding — breastfeeding or formula feeding — to be like in terms of ease, support, and how you'd feel about it? And what was the reality of feeding in the early weeks?

probes.probe_text: Was there a gap between the kind of feeding support you were offered and the kind of support you actually needed?
Did you feel judged — by professionals, family, or others — for your feeding choices or struggles? How did that affect you?
Did you turn to online communities or apps for feeding support? What made those more or less helpful than formal sources?

questions.question_text: Before your baby arrived, what did you expect your emotional and mental health to be like in the postpartum period? And what was your actual emotional experience in the weeks and months after birth?

probes.probe_text: Was there a gap between what you were feeling and what you felt you were 'allowed' to feel — by professionals, family, or yourself?
Were you ever screened or asked about your mental health postnatally? How was that handled — did it feel meaningful or routine?
Were there barriers — practical, cultural, or relational — that stopped you from seeking support when you were struggling emotionally?

questions.question_text: Looking across your entire maternity journey — from trying to conceive through to where you are now — what did you expect the overall experience of maternity care to deliver? And reflecting on the whole journey, what was the most significant gap between what you expected and what you received?

probes.probe_text: If you could change one thing about how the maternity care system is designed — not just what individual providers do, but how the system itself works — what would it be?
Was there a single moment across the whole journey where you felt most respected and cared for as a whole person? And a moment where you felt least so?
What would you tell someone at the very start of this journey about what to expect and what to watch out for?
